summary: Aims to unite regionally operated X.400 services on different continents into one GO-MHS Community from the end user's point of view, setting operational requirements for management domains. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Mail services in different parts of the world agree on rules so they act like one big system.

subtitle: Rules for connecting global X.400 email services into one community.

tldr.problem: Regional X.400 email services on different continents used different technologies and had no agreed way to route mail between each other or to Internet SMTP systems, fragmenting the global email community.
tldr.mechanism: The GO-MHS Community defines a common set of operational requirements: standard address formats, routing through RELAY-MTAs, support for multiple transport stacks, and mapping rules between X.400 and RFC-822 addresses.
tldr.outcome: X.400 services can now interconnect into one global GO-MHS community from the end user's perspective, allowing seamless email between regional services and the Internet.

facts.label: Address hierarchy levels
facts.value: 7 (Country, ADMD, PRMD, O, OU, PN, DDA)

facts.label: Required address elements
facts.value: Country, at least one of (PRMD/O/OU/PN), at least one of (PN/DDA)

today: RFC 1649 is an Informational RFC. It documents the operational requirements for X.400 services to participate in a global community. While X.400 email has largely been superseded by SMTP in most regions, this RFC captures the standards effort to make X.400 a viable global system during the 1990s.

sections.title: Linking X.400 Services Globally
sections.content:
Large operational X.400 message handling services already existed in the early 1990s, such as the COSINE MHS Service in Europe and the XNREN service in the US. Many organizations using these services were also connecting to the Internet. The goal was to create a Global Open Message Handling System (GO-MHS) Community where users connected to any regional X.400 service could send email to users in other regions and to RFC-822 (SMTP) users on the Internet, as if they were all part of one system.

This required agreement on minimum operational requirements. National X.400 service providers would implement these requirements, ensuring that organizations subscribing to X.400 in different countries could exchange messages with each other and with Internet users. The document addresses X.400 1984 and 1988 versions and the process for downgrading between them.
sections.eli5: Europe had one email system (X.400), the US had another (also X.400), and both wanted to talk to the Internet. This is how they agreed to make it work.

sections.title: How Management Domains Work
sections.content:
X.400 services are organized into Management Domains (MDs), of which there are two types. An Administration Management Domain (ADMD) is typically run by a national authority or telecommunications carrier. A Private Management Domain (PRMD) is run by an organization. The GO-MHS model allows any combination: countries with one ADMD, countries with PRMDs independent of any ADMD, or countries where PRMDs connect to ADMDs.

Each MD acts as a mail relay point. The document introduces the RELAY-MTA concept: one MTA (Message Transfer Agent) in each MD that handles mail destined for that MD when the final destination MTA is unknown. This enables routing without needing a complete table of every MTA in every MD. The RELAY-MTA accepts responsibility for all messages to well-defined recipients in its domain and uses the same routing rules regardless of the transport stack used (TCP/IP, CLNP, X.25, or others).
sections.eli5: Big organizations and countries each run their own mail system (a Management Domain). Each has a main post office called RELAY-MTA that knows how to get mail to the right place.

sections.title: X.400 Address Registration
sections.content:
For mail to route correctly across the GO-MHS Community, addresses must follow a strict hierarchy. Each address includes Country (C), Administration Domain Name (ADMD), optionally a Private Domain Name (PRMD), Organization (O), optionally Organizational Units (OUs), a Personal Name (PN), and optionally Domain-Defined Attributes (DDAs). At least one of PRMD, O, OU or PN must be present, and at least one of PN or DDA must be present.

Country codes come from ISO 3166. Each level must be unique within its parent level. For example, an OU is unique within its Organization. The document also defines how to handle personal names: if surnames are not unique within an organization, given names and initials must be used to disambiguate. To help with later mapping to Internet email, the names should use only letters, digits, and minus signs, without spaces.
sections.eli5: Every email address is built like a postal address: Country, Company, Department, Person. That way, mail routers know exactly where to look.

sections.title: Bridging X.400 and Internet Email
sections.content:
Organizations with both X.400 users and Internet RFC-822 email users must be able to send to each other. If an X.400 organization has registered in the GO-MHS address space, it can share an address space with its RFC-822 users. For example, a university's X.400 and RFC-822 users can both use the same organizational hierarchy (C=US; ADMD=Internet; PRMD=XNREN; O=UW-Madison; OU=cs), with the personal part differing only in how the name is encoded.

For organizations without a defined X.400 address space, Domain-Defined Attributes (DDAs) are used. An X.400 user can address an RFC-822 recipient using an RFC-822 DDA (for example, DD.RFC-822=user@some.place.edu). RFC-822 users addressing X.400 recipients either use a standard email address (if the organization has registered), or use an escape-encoded form with the full X.400 address in the local part: /G=FirstName/S=LastName/O=org/C=us/@gateway.edu.
sections.eli5: If your company uses both email systems, mail goes to the same mailbox either way. If it doesn't, you write the address in a special format that both systems understand.

sections.title: Routing and Operations
sections.content:
The GO-MHS Community uses two key documents to organize routing. The RELAY-MTA document lists the names and connection data of RELAY-MTAs, including their supported protocol stacks and X.400 versions. The Domain document lists sub-tree hierarchies of X.400 addresses and the MTAs willing to accept mail for those addresses, with priority values for choosing among multiple routes.

These documents are coordinated centrally and must be globally consistent to ensure reliable routing before a full X.500 directory infrastructure is deployed. The GO-MHS Community document contains the central coordination point's contact information, file server addresses, and the mandatory and optional networks and stacks for the community. Finally, each MTA should collect basic statistics on message flow (dates, times, sizes, routing information) to help with network management and troubleshooting.
sections.eli5: One document lists all the mail post offices and how to reach them. Another lists which addresses each post office handles. That way, every mail router knows the right path.
